title: A product or project manager's first day
audience: Someone who plans, tracks and reports rather than writes code. Plain words throughout.

steps.goal: Pick the project up where it was left
steps.see: A short summary of PizzaBot 3000: what it is, what was decided, what is open, and a question about where to start.
steps.why: You never re-read old notes to find your place; the summary is built from the project's own files.

steps.see: Up to three lines: the one task to do now, why it is the one, and a command to try after it.
steps.why: When everything feels urgent, one clear next step beats a list.

steps.goal: See what is waiting on you
steps.see: Your open tasks, most urgent first, with due dates and anything waiting on someone.
steps.why: Overdue and waiting items are the ones that slip; this shows them without opening a spreadsheet.

steps.goal: Add a task in one sentence
steps.say: /gt:gt-create task Send the stakeholder update by Friday
steps.see: One new line under the project's Tasks, with the date understood from your words.
steps.why: A task written now is a task not forgotten at 5 pm.

steps.say: Write down a decision: we cap the negotiation at three rounds, because longer rounds lost customers
steps.see: A short decision record: what was decided, why, and what was rejected, filed in the project.
steps.why: In three months nobody remembers why; the record does.

steps.say: /gt:gt-query what did we decide about negotiation rounds
steps.see: The answer in a sentence or two, with the note it came from.
steps.why: Your notes answer questions so you do not have to ask a colleague twice.

steps.see: A plain brief of what moved, what was decided and what is blocked, then the notes saved and a handoff if anything is unfinished.
steps.why: Tomorrow's session starts from what you learned today, not from a blank page.
